module_title: Financial Management for Your Essential Oil Business

lessons.title: Calculating Costs of Production per Bottle
lessons.body:
To know if your essential oil business is making money, you must first know exactly what each bottle costs you to produce. This is called your cost of production per bottle. Start by listing all your direct costs for one batch. For example, suppose you harvest 100 kg of lemongrass. You pay 5,000 KES for the harvest labour. You rent a distiller for 3,000 KES. You use 500 KES of firewood and 200 KES of water. That batch yields 500 ml of oil. Your total direct cost is 8,700 KES. If you fill 10 ml bottles, you get 50 bottles. So the oil cost per bottle is 8,700 / 50 = 174 KES. Now add packaging: each 10 ml amber bottle with dropper costs 60 KES, label 10 KES, and a small box 20 KES. So packaging adds 90 KES per bottle. Your total cost per bottle is 174 + 90 = 264 KES.

But thatâs not all. You also have indirect costs: your time, transport to buy bottles, market stall fees, and a portion of your phone and internet for marketing. If you spend 10 hours per week on the business, value your time at 200 KES per hour. If you produce 50 bottles per week, thatâs 2,000 KES labour divided by 50 = 40 KES per bottle. Add transport 500 KES and stall fee 1,000 KES per week, divided by 50 = 30 KES per bottle. So total indirect cost per bottle = 40 + 30 = 70 KES. Your full cost per bottle is 264 + 70 = 334 KES.

Write this down for each product: lemongrass, eucalyptus, tea tree. Keep a notebook or a simple Excel sheet on your phone. Update it every time prices change. Once you know your true cost, you can set a price that covers everything and leaves a profit. Without this number, you might sell at a loss and not even know it.

lessons.title: Setting Profitable Prices for Different Products
lessons.body:
Once you know your cost per bottle, you can set a price that gives you a healthy profit. A simple rule is to multiply your cost by a markup. For direct sales to friends and local customers, a 2x markup is common. If your cost is 334 KES, you sell at 668 KES. For wholesale to shops, use a 1.5x markup: 334 x 1.5 = 501 KES, so you might sell at 500 KES. But donât just copy others. Check what similar oils sell for in your area. If your lemongrass oil is high quality, you can charge more.

Different products can have different markups. For example, a 10 ml bottle of tea tree oil might cost you 400 KES to produce. You could sell it for 800 KES retail. But a 50 ml bottle of eucalyptus oil might cost 1,200 KES and you sell for 2,400 KES. The key is to always cover your full cost and then add profit. Never price below cost, even to friends. Instead, offer a small discount like 10% for bulk orders of 5 bottles or more.

Also consider your market. In cities like Nairobi or Lagos, customers may pay more than in rural areas. If you sell online, add shipping costs to the price. A good strategy is to have three price points: a small 10 ml bottle for trial at a low price (but still above cost), a medium 30 ml bottle as your best seller, and a large 100 ml bottle for serious users. This way, you cater to different budgets and increase sales. Review your prices every three months. If your costs go up, raise prices. Donât be afraid to charge what you are worth.

lessons.title: Keeping Simple Records of Sales and Expenses
lessons.body:
You donât need accounting software to keep good records. A simple notebook and a pen work perfectly. Divide a page into two columns: one for money coming in (sales) and one for money going out (expenses). Every time you sell a bottle, write the date, what you sold, and how much you received. Every time you buy bottles, labels, or pay for transport, write the date, what you bought, and how much you spent. At the end of each week, add up both columns. The difference is your profit or loss for that week.

For example, in one week you sell 20 bottles of lemongrass oil at 700 KES each = 14,000 KES. You also sell 10 bottles of eucalyptus at 800 KES = 8,000 KES. Total sales = 22,000 KES. Your expenses: bottles and labels 4,000 KES, transport 1,000 KES, market stall 2,000 KES, and a new distiller part 3,000 KES. Total expenses = 10,000 KES. Your profit for the week is 22,000 - 10,000 = 12,000 KES. Write this summary at the bottom of the page.

Keep all receipts in a small envelope or plastic folder. If you use a phone, you can take photos of receipts and keep them in a folder. At the end of the month, transfer the weekly totals to a monthly summary. This helps you see trends: which products sell best, which months are slow, and where you can cut costs. Good records also help you get loans or grants later, because lenders want to see that you are organized. Start todayâeven a single page per week is enough.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow in a Small Business
lessons.body:
Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. Even if you are making a profit on paper, you can run out of cash if you donât manage it well. For example, you might sell 50 bottles on credit to a shop, meaning they pay you next month. But you need to buy bottles and pay your workers this week. If you have no cash, you canât produce more oil. So cash flow is about timing.

To manage cash flow, first track when money comes in and when it goes out. Use a simple cash flow calendar. Draw a table with columns for each week. In each week, write expected sales (cash you will receive) and expected expenses (cash you must pay). For example, Week 1: sales 10,000 KES, expenses 8,000 KES, net cash +2,000 KES. Week 2: sales 5,000 KES, expenses 12,000 KES (because you buy a bulk order of bottles), net cash -7,000 KES. If you see a negative week coming, plan ahead. You could delay buying bottles, ask for a deposit from customers, or arrange a short-term loan from a savings group.

Always keep a cash reserveâat least enough to cover one month of essential expenses. Build this slowly by setting aside 10% of every sale. Also, encourage cash sales. If you sell on credit, ask for a 50% deposit upfront. And pay your suppliers on time but not early, unless they offer a discount. Review your cash flow weekly. If you see a problem, act immediately: reduce spending, increase sales, or find a small bridge loan. Good cash flow management keeps your business alive even when sales are slow.

lessons.title: Saving and Reinvesting Profits for Growth
lessons.body:
Profit is what is left after you pay all your costs. It is not your salaryâit is the fuel for growth. Many small producers make the mistake of spending all profit on personal needs. Instead, follow the 50-30-20 rule: 50% of profit reinvested in the business, 30% as your pay, and 20% saved for emergencies. For example, if you make 20,000 KES profit in a month, put 10,000 KES back into the business, take 6,000 KES as your income, and save 4,000 KES in a separate account or a locked box.

Reinvesting means buying better equipment, more raw materials, or marketing. For instance, you could buy a larger distiller to increase production, or purchase a bulk order of bottles at a lower price. You could also pay for a booth at a local trade fair. Each reinvestment should help you earn more next month. Keep a list of reinvestment ideas and their cost. Start with the one that gives the fastest return.

Saving is also crucial. Open a separate savings account at a SACCO or mobile money account. Aim to save at least three months of business expenses. This protects you when a distiller breaks or when lemongrass harvest is poor. You can also use savings to take advantage of opportunities, like a large order that requires upfront cash. Review your profit and savings every month. As your business grows, increase your reinvestment percentage. For example, after one year, you might move to 60% reinvestment, 20% pay, and 20% savings. This discipline turns a small business into a thriving enterprise.

lessons.title: Accessing Microfinance and Grants for Small Producers
lessons.body:
When you need money to grow, you have several options: microfinance loans, grants, and savings groups. Microfinance institutions (MFIs) like Kiva, BRAC, or local SACCOs offer small loans to entrepreneurs. They usually require a business plan, records of sales and expenses, and sometimes collateral or a group guarantee. Before applying, prepare a simple one-page plan: what you do, your costs, your profits, and how much you need and why. For example, you might ask for 50,000 KES to buy a new distiller that will double your production. Show that you can repay 5,000 KES per month from increased sales.

Grants are free money, but they are competitive. Look for grants from NGOs, government programs, or agricultural development agencies. For essential oils, check with organizations like the Africa Enterprise Challenge Fund, or local offices of GIZ, USAID, or the Food and Agriculture Organization. They often have calls for proposals. You will need a clear budget and a plan for how the grant will help you create jobs or increase income for your community. Keep your records clean and take photos of your work.

Another option is a savings group (also called a merry-go-round or table banking). You and other producers contribute a fixed amount weekly or monthly, and members take turns receiving the lump sum. This is low-cost and builds trust. You can also ask for a small loan from the group. To succeed with any funding, be honest, keep promises, and repay on time. Start small: borrow 10,000 KES, repay it, then borrow more. Good credit history opens bigger doors.

quiz.q: What is the first step to calculate your cost of production per bottle?
options: A) Add up all direct costs for one batch
quiz.explanation: You must know your direct costs before you can determine cost per bottle.

quiz.q: If a batch yields 500 ml and you fill 10 ml bottles, how many bottles do you get?
quiz.explanation: 500 ml divided by 10 ml per bottle equals 50 bottles.

quiz.q: Which of these is an indirect cost?
quiz.explanation: Your time is an indirect cost because it is not directly tied to a single bottle but supports production.

quiz.q: Why should you update your cost calculation regularly?
options: B) Because prices of inputs change
C) To make it look complicated
quiz.explanation: Input prices like bottles, labour, and transport can change, so your cost per bottle changes too.

quiz.q: If your total cost per bottle is 334 KES and you use a 2x markup, what is your selling price?
quiz.explanation: 2 times 334 equals 668 KES.

quiz.q: What markup is suggested for wholesale to shops?
quiz.explanation: A 1.5x markup is common for wholesale to keep prices competitive.

quiz.q: Why is it bad to price below cost even for friends?
quiz.explanation: Selling below cost means you are paying to give away your product, which harms your business.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy for different product sizes?
options: B) Three price points: small, medium, large
quiz.explanation: Having three price points caters to different budgets and increases sales.

quiz.q: How often should you review your prices?
quiz.explanation: Reviewing every three months helps you adjust to cost changes and market conditions.

quiz.q: What is the simplest tool for keeping records?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are simple, cheap, and effective for basic record-keeping.

quiz.q: In a sales and expenses record, what goes in the 'money in' column?
quiz.explanation: Sales are money coming into the business.

quiz.q: Why keep receipts?
options: A) To prove expenses and for loan applications
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide evidence of expenses and are often required for loans or grants.

quiz.q: What does a weekly profit summary show?
options: C) Difference between sales and expenses
quiz.explanation: Profit is sales minus expenses, so the summary shows that difference.

quiz.q: What is cash flow?
options: A) The movement of money in and out
quiz.explanation: Cash flow tracks when money comes in and goes out, not just profit.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
options: A) Because sales are on credit and expenses are due now
B) Because profit is not real
D) Because they don't keep records
quiz.explanation: Timing mismatches between cash inflows and outflows can cause a cash shortage even if profitable.

quiz.q: What is a cash flow calendar used for?
options: A) To track expected sales and expenses weekly
quiz.explanation: It helps you see weeks when cash may be negative and plan ahead.

quiz.q: How can you handle a negative cash flow week?
options: A) Delay buying bottles, ask for deposits, or get a small loan
quiz.explanation: These actions help bridge the gap until cash comes in.

quiz.q: What is a good cash reserve target?
options: B) One month of essential expenses
quiz.explanation: One month of essential expenses is a practical cushion for small businesses.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sell on credit?
options: A) Ask for a 50% deposit upfront
quiz.explanation: A deposit reduces the risk of non-payment and improves cash flow.

quiz.q: What is the 50-30-20 rule for profit?
quiz.explanation: This rule balances growth, personal income, and emergency savings.

quiz.q: Why is reinvesting profit important?
options: A) It helps the business grow and earn more
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Reinvestment buys better equipment, materials, and marketing to increase future profits.

quiz.q: Where should you keep your savings?
options: A) In a separate account or locked box
quiz.explanation: A separate account or locked box reduces the temptation to spend savings.

quiz.q: How much should you aim to save for emergencies?
options: B) Three months of business expenses
quiz.explanation: Three months of expenses provides a safety net for unexpected events.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of saving for your business?
options: A) You can take advantage of opportunities
C) You can lend to friends
D) You can buy personal items
quiz.explanation: Savings allow you to act quickly on bulk discounts or large orders.

quiz.q: What do microfinance institutions typically require?
options: A) A business plan and records
quiz.explanation: MFIs want to see that you have a viable business and can repay.

quiz.q: What is a grant?
options: A) Free money that does not need to be repaid
quiz.explanation: Grants are funds given for a specific purpose and are not repaid.

quiz.q: Where can you find grants for small producers?
options: A) NGOs, government programs, and development agencies
quiz.explanation: Many organizations offer grants to support small businesses and agricultural producers.

quiz.q: What is a savings group?
options: A) A group where members contribute and take turns receiving lump sums
quiz.explanation: Savings groups pool money and rotate the lump sum among members.

quiz.q: How can you build good credit history?
options: A) Borrow small amounts and repay on time
quiz.explanation: Starting small and repaying promptly demonstrates reliability to lenders.

quiz.q: What should you include in a one-page business plan for a loan?
options: A) What you do, costs, profits, and loan purpose
quiz.explanation: Lenders want a clear summary of your business and how the loan will be used.

quiz.q: Why is honesty important when applying for funding?
options: A) It builds trust and improves your chances
C) It helps you get more money
D) It is required by law only
quiz.explanation: Funders value integrity and are more likely to support honest applicants.
